title: Ecosystem Indicator Workflows Development Plan
text:
Executive summary
The Ecosystem Indicator Workflows (EIW) project aims to establish a sustainable framework for the development, sharing, and reuse of ecosystem-specific indicators through documented, reproducible, and modular computational workflows. The project responds to a growing need for transparent and scalable approaches to ecosystem assessment, monitoring, reporting, conservation planning, ecosystem accounting, and environmental decision-making.
Ecosystem indicators are increasingly used to understand ecosystem condition, measure ecological change, support environmental reporting, and track progress towards national and international biodiversity objectives. However, the methods used to develop these indicators are often developed independently for specific projects, resulting in duplicated effort, limited reproducibility, inconsistent documentation, and challenges in adapting workflows to new ecosystems and applications.
The EIW project addresses these challenges through the development of a common workflow framework that supports the creation of fit-for-purpose ecosystem indicators. Each workflow is designed to begin with a user-defined scope, including the definition of a target ecosystem, intended purpose, diagnostic mechanism, and indicator variable. Workflows follow a consistent structure comprising ecosystem data preparation, indicator data preparation, indicator calculation, and validation and uncertainty assessment. To promote scientific consistency and interoperability, ecosystem definitions are aligned with the IUCN Global Ecosystem Typology and workflows are designed to follow FAIR and reproducible research principles.
This Development Plan presents the outcomes of the project’s requirements gathering activities and defines a two-year roadmap for workflow development. Requirements were collected through stakeholder workshops, consultations, interviews, and engagement activities involving researchers, ecologists, software developers, data scientists, environmental managers, government agencies, infrastructure providers, and other prospective users of ecosystem indicator workflows. These activities identified strong demand for workflows that are adaptable, transparent, interoperable, well-documented, and easy to reuse across different ecosystem types and assessment contexts.
The plan identifies nine primary user groups and a series of priority use cases spanning indicator development, environmental reporting, ecosystem accounting, environmental management, workflow publication, workflow discovery, training, and nature-related reporting applications. These use cases provide the basis for prioritising workflow functionality and establishing a staged delivery roadmap.
The roadmap is structured around two development tranches. The first tranche focuses on establishing the foundational components of the workflow ecosystem, including a modular workflow architecture, ecosystem and indicator data preparation workflows, data harmonisation approaches, validation methods, demonstration workflows, metadata standards, and introductory training resources. The second tranche focuses on scaling and operationalising the workflow ecosystem through the development of workflow catalogues, enhanced interoperability services, vocabulary crosswalks, FAIR-compliant workflow publication, advanced training resources, and expanded workflow coverage.
The Development Plan also establishes a framework for ongoing review and prioritisation. Functionality planned for the second development tranche will be reviewed during the fourth quarter of Year 1 to ensure that future development continues to reflect user needs, technological opportunities, and emerging ecosystem assessment requirements. This adaptive approach recognises that user requirements, data availability, policy demands, and scientific methods will continue to evolve throughout the life of the project.
Ultimately, the EIW project seeks to build more than a collection of workflows. It aims to establish a community-supported toolbox of reusable methods, software, data resources, and training materials that enable ecosystem indicators to be developed, shared, adapted, and maintained across organisations, disciplines, and jurisdictions. By embedding principles of reproducibility, transparency, interoperability, and reuse throughout the workflow lifecycle, the project will support more consistent and accessible ecosystem indicator development for research, management, policy, and reporting applications.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 Background
Ecosystem-specific indicators are used to support ecosystem assessment, monitoring, reporting, conservation planning, ecosystem accounting, and environmental decision-making. These indicators provide a structured way to measure ecosystem characteristics, assess ecological condition, track change through time, and evaluate progress towards management and policy objectives.
Despite their growing importance, the development of ecosystem indicators is often hampered by fragmented analytical approaches, inconsistent methods, poorly documented workflows, and challenges associated with integrating diverse data sources. Indicator development frequently relies on bespoke analyses that are difficult to reproduce, adapt to new contexts, or apply consistently across ecosystem types. These limitations reduce transparency, constrain scalability, and hinder the uptake of ecosystem indicators by the broader research, policy, and management communities.
The Ecosystem Indicator Workflows (EIW) project was established to address these challenges through the development of modular, transparent, and reproducible workflows that support the creation of ecosystem-specific indicators. The project aims to enable users to develop fit-for-purpose indicators by combining ecological expertise, data resources, computational workflows, and reproducible research practices within a common framework.

title: 2  Requirements Gathering Activities
text:
2.3 Participants in requirement gathering activities
We had 32 participants in the first stakeholder workshop that involved ecosystem scientists, data analysts, government practitioners, research software engineers, data managers, and platform providers. We had 12 participants in the second workshop that targeted researchers with direct experience in ecosystem assessments. We gathered feedback through participation in 18 meetings with different participants from government, data scientists, platform providers, and researchers and students.

title: 3  User Groups
text:
The Ecosystem Indicator Workflow (EIW) program serves a diverse community of users with different technical capabilities, responsibilities, and objectives. User groups were identified through stakeholder workshops, requirements gathering activities, market analysis, and community engagement planning.
The user groups described below represent the primary audiences for workflow development, testing, adoption, and long-term sustainability.









ID
User Type
Description
Primary Interaction




UG01
Ecologist / Conservation Scientist
Subject-matter expert responsible for defining ecological concepts, ecosystem boundaries, diagnostic mechanisms, and indicator variables. Typically familiar with ecosystem classification systems such as the IUCN Global Ecosystem Typology and ecosystem assessment frameworks. Technical skills vary considerably.
Defines workflow scope; identifies indicator requirements; reviews assumptions; validates indicator outputs; contributes ecological expertise throughout workflow development.


UG02
Student / Early-Career Researcher
Learner and emerging practitioner using workflows as educational and skill-development resources. Often has limited experience with ecosystem indicators, reproducible workflows, or scientific programming.
Participates in training; runs demonstration workflows; contributes testing and documentation feedback; develops workflow skills through worked examples and guided exercises.


UG03
Environmental Manager / Technical Practitioner
Operational user applying ecosystem indicators to support ecosystem management, conservation planning, monitoring programs, natural resource management, restoration activities, or environmental assessments. May work in government, NGOs, Indigenous organisations, or consultancies.
Executes workflows or uses workflow outputs to support management decisions; provides feedback on usability and operational requirements; contributes use cases and validation examples.


UG04
Environmental Policy Analyst / Reporting Officer
User of ecosystem indicators for policy development, environmental reporting, ecosystem accounting, State of the Environment reporting, biodiversity monitoring, and compliance obligations. Typically consumes workflow outputs rather than running workflows directly.
Accesses indicator outputs, reports, metadata, and provenance records; evaluates indicators for policy and reporting purposes; identifies emerging reporting requirements.


UG05
Environmental Consultant / Assurance Practitioner
Professional user applying ecosystem indicators within environmental consulting, auditing, sustainability reporting, ecosystem accounting, and nature-related disclosure activities. Includes organisations supporting TNFD and related reporting frameworks.
Uses workflow outputs and methods to support client assessments; adapts workflows to project-specific requirements; contributes implementation feedback and industry use cases.


UG06
Data Scientist / Technical Analyst
Technical practitioner who applies, adapts, and extends workflows for research, monitoring, and assessment purposes. Typically uses R, Python, GIS tools, and statistical workflows.
Runs workflows using new datasets; adapts workflows for new ecosystems or assessment purposes; performs data preparation and quality assurance; develops new workflow components.


UG07
Research Software Engineer (RSE) / Workflow Developer
Technical specialist responsible for designing, implementing, maintaining, and documenting workflows. Develops reproducible computational methods, modular workflow components, and software infrastructure.
Develops workflow code; manages repositories; implements FAIR practices; maintains software environments; contributes documentation and workflow standards.


UG08
Data Provider / Data Custodian
Organisation or individual responsible for generating, managing, or publishing ecosystem and indicator datasets. Includes government agencies, monitoring programs, research infrastructures, and repository managers.
Provides authoritative datasets; supports metadata and provenance requirements; advises on data quality, limitations, licensing, and update schedules.


UG09
Platform Administrator / Research Infrastructure Provider
Technical personnel responsible for workflow deployment, hosting, security, interoperability, performance, and long-term infrastructure support. Includes providers of cloud, HPC, and research infrastructure platforms.
Deploys workflow environments; manages containerised infrastructure; supports interoperability, authentication, monitoring, and operational sustainability.


UG10
Science Communicator and Trainer
Translates ecosystem indicator outputs and methods into accessible formats for diverse audiences (educators, outreach officers, training coordinators). Strong in communication/pedagogy; may have limited technical background.
Converts outputs into plain-language summaries, visuals, and training materials; bridges technical developers (UG06/UG07) and non-technical users (UG03/UG04); gathers feedback to improve accessibility.

title: 4  User Requirements for Ecosystem Indicator Workflows
text:
4.1 Overview
Workshop participants explored a series of realistic workflow development scenarios and identified user needs, technical challenges, and priorities for future Ecosystem Indicator Workflows (EIWs).
Workshop participants consistently emphasised that the value of Ecosystem Indicator Workflows extends beyond indicator calculation. Users require workflows that are adaptable, reproducible, transparent, well-documented, and capable of integrating diverse ecosystem datasets while remaining accessible to users with varying technical capabilities.
crumbs: 4  User Requirements for Ecosystem Indicator Workflows

title: 4  User Requirements for Ecosystem Indicator Workflows
text:
4.2 Considerations for user requirements

4.2.1 Workflow Adaptability
Users require workflows that can be adapted to different ecosystem types, geographic regions, and assessment purposes without requiring complete redevelopment. Stakeholders identified adaptability as one of the most important requirements for the initiative.
Participants repeatedly highlighted that existing workflows are often difficult to repurpose because ecosystem-specific assumptions and methods are embedded throughout the workflow rather than isolated in configurable components.



4.2.2 Reproducibility and Transparency
Users require workflows that can be independently reproduced, verified, and maintained over time. Reproducibility was identified as a core requirement underpinning scientific credibility and long-term adoption.
Users highlighted challenges associated with legacy workflows, undocumented dependencies, restricted data access, and software version incompatibilities. Participants identified containerisation and explicit environment management as important mechanisms for maintaining reproducibility.



4.2.3 Data Discovery, Access and Integration
Users require workflows that simplify the process of locating, understanding, accessing, and combining ecosystem and indicator datasets from multiple sources. Data preparation was consistently identified as the most time-consuming component of indicator development.
Participants highlighted common challenges including fragmented datasets, inconsistent survey methodologies, varying spatial resolutions, uneven geographic coverage, and difficulties obtaining access to restricted datasets.



4.2.4 Classification and Vocabulary Alignment
Users require ecosystem workflows that support alignment between national ecosystem classifications and international standards.
Stakeholders identified ecosystem classification mapping as one of the largest barriers to workflow development and noted that a substantial proportion of effort is currently spent reconciling classification systems across jurisdictions and assessment frameworks.



4.2.5 Documentation, Training and Knowledge Transfer
Users require documentation and training resources that accommodate varying levels of technical expertise.
Participants consistently identified documentation and training as critical enablers of workflow adoption. Requirements varied across user groups, but all groups emphasised the need for high-quality documentation and practical examples.



4.2.6 Accessibility and Usability
Users require workflows that minimise technical barriers to adoption while supporting a diverse user community.
Workshop participants demonstrated strong familiarity with R, Python, RStudio, QGIS, and Jupyter-based environments, while familiarity with specialised platforms and workflow technologies varied considerably. As a result, workflow design should prioritise accessibility and user experience over technical complexity where practical.



4.2.7 Validation, Uncertainty and Scientific Confidence
Users require workflows that support the transparent evaluation of indicator quality and reliability.
Participants noted that uncertainty information is frequently omitted from final products despite being critical for interpretation and decision-making. Validation approaches and integration of expert judgement were identified as areas requiring greater consistency across workflows.

title: 4  User Requirements for Ecosystem Indicator Workflows
text:
4.3 Priority User Requirements
Across all workshops, the following requirements emerged as the highest priorities for the Ecosystem Indicator Workflow program:

Adaptable and modular workflow architecture.
Reproducible workflows supported by version-controlled computational environments.
Alignment with the IUCN Global Ecosystem Typology and other recognised standards.
Transparent data provenance and metadata.
Guidance for integrating heterogeneous ecosystem datasets.
Comprehensive documentation and tiered training materials.
Explicit treatment of validation, uncertainty, and expert judgement.
FAIR-compliant workflows, tools, metadata, and outputs.

Requirements 1 to 7 provide the foundation for prioritising workflow functionality and defining the staged delivery roadmap described in subsequent sections of this document. Requirement 8 is embedded in all activities of the project.

title: 5  High-Level Workflow Requirements and Constraints
text:
5.1 Purpose
Ecosystem Indicator Workflows (EIWs) are documented, transparent, and reproducible computational workflows developed to generate ecosystem-specific and fit-for-purpose indicators. The workflows are intended to support consistent indicator development across ecosystem types while providing sufficient flexibility to address different management, monitoring, assessment and reporting needs.
All workflows are designed to align with FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable) and support reproducible research practices.
crumbs: 5  High-Level Workflow Requirements and Constraints

title: 5  High-Level Workflow Requirements and Constraints
text:
5.2 Scope and Structure
The development of an Ecosystem Indicator Workflow must begin with a clearly defined scope. The scope establishes the context, purpose and intended application of the workflow and provides the basis for all subsequent workflow development activities.
Each workflow must define the following four attributes:

Target Ecosystem Definition: The workflow must identify the ecosystem or ecosystem group that will be assessed.
Intended Purpose: The workflow must clearly state the purpose of the indicator and the decision-making context in which it will be used. Examples may include: Environmental reporting, Natural capital accounting, Ecosystem risk assessment, Ecosystem recovery and integrity assessment, Conservation planning.
Diagnostic Mechanism: The workflow must describe the ecological mechanism through which the selected indicator provides information about ecosystem status, condition or change.
Indicator Variable Selection: The workflow must identify one or more measurable variables that can be used to quantify the selected ecosystem characteristic.

All Ecosystem Indicator Workflows will follow a common modular structure consisting of four core workflow components.

Ecosystem Data Preparation: This module prepares ecosystem spatial data and associated ecosystem information required for indicator calculation. Dataset selection decisions must be documented and justified.
Indicator Data Preparation: This module prepares the data required to quantify the selected indicator variable. All processing steps must be transparent and reproducible.
Indicator Calculation: This module implements the analytical methods required to generate the ecosystem indicator. Calculation methods should be designed to allow consistent application across assessment periods where appropriate.
Validation and Uncertainty Assessment: This module assesses the performance, reliability and limitations of the indicator. Validation outcomes must be documented alongside indicator results.
crumbs: 5  High-Level Workflow Requirements and Constraints

title: 5  High-Level Workflow Requirements and Constraints
text:
5.3 Design Principles
The Ecosystem Indicator Workflow program will be guided by the following principles:

Scientific credibility – indicators are based on sound ecological understanding and defensible methods.
Fitness for purpose – indicators are developed to address clearly defined user needs and decision contexts.
Transparency – methods, assumptions and data sources are fully documented.
Reproducibility – workflows can be repeated and independently verified.
Interoperability – workflows align with recognised standards and classification frameworks.
Scalability – workflows can be adapted to additional ecosystems and indicator types over time.
Accessibility – tools and outputs are usable by a broad community of researchers, practitioners and decision makers.
Continuous improvement – workflows can be updated as new data, methods and user requirements emerge.
crumbs: 5  High-Level Workflow Requirements and Constraints

title: 5  High-Level Workflow Requirements and Constraints
text:
5.4 High-Level Workflow Requirements

5.4.1 Scope Definition Requirements

ScopeRequirements

    Target Ecosystem Definition

1.1Ecosystem definitions must align with the IUCN Global Ecosystem Typology.
1.2The ecosystem classification level must be appropriate to the intended application of the indicator.
1.3The ecosystem definition must be documented and traceable throughout the workflow.
Intended Purpose
2.1The workflow must clearly state the purpose of the indicator. 
2.2The workflow must clearly state the decision-making context in which it will be used. 
2.3The intended purpose must guide data selection, methodology and validation requirements.
Diagnostic Mechanism
3.1The diagnostic mechanism should document the ecological process being assessed
3.2The diagnostic mechanism should document the relationship between the indicator and ecosystem characteristics
3.3The diagnostic mechanism should document key assumptions underpinning indicator interpretation
Indicator Variable Selection
4.1Indicator variables should be scientifically defensible
4.2Indicator variables should be measurable using available data sources.
4.3Indicator variables should be appropriate to the intended purpose.
4.4Indicator variables should support repeatable assessment through time.



5.4.2 Workflow Structure Requirements

ModuleCodeRequirements

    Ecosystem Data Preparation

1.1Identification and acquisition of ecosystem datasets.
1.2Documentation of ecosystem classification systems and mapping methods.
1.3Standardisation and preprocessing of ecosystem spatial data.
1.4Recording of all assumptions and transformations applied to source data.
1.5aWhere available, ecosystem datasets should utilise the best available information from State and Territory jurisdictions.
1.5bFederal spatial datasets or global datasets may be used when: (a) They provide a better fit for the intended purpose; (b) Regional or jurisdictional datasets are unavailable; and/or (c) Regional datasets lack sufficient coverage, consistency or quality.

    Indicator Data Preparation

2.1Identification and acquisition of indicator datasets.
2.2Assessment of data quality and suitability.
2.3Documentation of data provenance.
2.4Data cleaning, transformation and standardisation.
2.5Management of temporal and spatial alignment between ecosystem and indicator datasets.


    Indicator Calculation

3.1Documentation of all mathematical and analytical methods.
3.2Explicit parameter definitions.
3.3Recording of assumptions and methodological choices.
3.4Repeatable execution using documented computational procedures.
3.5Generation of standard outputs suitable for interpretation and reporting.


    Validation and Uncertainty Assessment

4.1Validation against independent datasets where available.
4.2Documentation of methodological limitations.
4.3Identification of data quality issues and potential biases.
4.4Quantification of uncertainty where feasible.
4.5Transparent communication of confidence and limitations associated with outputs.



5.4.3 Software and Technical Requirements
The Ecosystem Indicator Workflow framework must be supported by software tools and computational environments that promote transparency, accessibility and reproducibility. Workflow implementation should minimise barriers to adoption and facilitate long-term maintenance.
This will be achieved through:

Use of open-access or widely accessible software where feasible.
Use of documented and version-controlled analytical processes.
Support for workflow portability across organisations and jurisdictions.
Ability to adapt workflows for alternative ecosystems and use cases.
Transparent documentation of software dependencies, packages and computational environments.



5.4.4 FAIR and Reproducibility Requirements
All workflows, tools and outputs must align with FAIR principles and reproducible research practices.

Findable
Workflow documentation, code, metadata and outputs should be discoverable through appropriate repositories and documentation systems.


Accessible
Workflow components and outputs should be accessible to authorised users through documented and sustainable access mechanisms.


Interoperable
Data, metadata and outputs should use recognised standards, formats and classification systems to support integration with other workflows, platforms and reporting systems.


Reusable
Workflow documentation must provide sufficient detail to enable independent application, review, adaptation and reuse by other practitioners.
crumbs: 5  High-Level Workflow Requirements and Constraints

title: 5  High-Level Workflow Requirements and Constraints
text:
5.5 Constraints
The development and implementation of Ecosystem Indicator Workflows will be subject to several constraints.

Data Availability

Indicator development is dependent on the availability, quality and coverage of ecosystem and indicator datasets.
Data availability will vary across ecosystem types, jurisdictions and time periods.
Some workflows may require the use of proxy variables where direct measurements are unavailable.

Data Consistency

Differences in spatial scale, classification systems, temporal coverage and collection methodologies may affect comparability across datasets.
Additional data harmonisation may be required to support national-scale assessments.

Computational Constraints

Computational methods should balance scientific rigour with practical implementation requirements.
Workflows should remain maintainable by future users and project teams.

Resource Constraints

Workflow development priorities must reflect available funding, staff capacity and stakeholder demand.
Not all desired functionality may be delivered within the initial development period.

Scientific Constraints

Ecological processes are inherently complex and may not be fully represented by individual indicators.
All indicators should clearly communicate assumptions, limitations and uncertainty associated with interpretation.

title: 6  Detailed Use cases
text:
6.1 Overview
Requirements gathering activities identified a range of user groups that will contribute to, operate, or consume Ecosystem Indicator Workflows (EIWs). The use cases below represent the most common and highest-priority applications identified through workshops, user stories, and stakeholder consultations. These use cases informed the prioritisation of workflow functionality and the staged development roadmap.

title: 6  Detailed Use cases
text:
6.2 Use case descriptions

UC01 – Adapt an existing fit-for-purpose ecosystem-specific indicator to make it reproducible







Attribute
Description




Primary User
Ecologist / Conservation Scientist (UG01)


Supporting Users
Research Software Engineer (UG07), Data Scientist (UG06)


Purpose
Adapt an ecosystem-specific indicator to make it reproducible


Trigger
Update existing ecosystem assessments, revisit research or monitoring questions.


Key requirements
AD01, AD02, AD05, RE01, RE02, RE04, VO01, VO02, DD02, DD03, DD04, DD06, DO04, AC01, AC03, VA02, VA03, VA04, VA05




Implementation steps

Check existing scope of the workflow as per high-level requirements: ecosystem, purpose, diagnostic and variable selection.
Check structure of the workflow as per high-level requirements: data preparation, calculation and validation/uncertainty assessment.
Assess existing gaps in implementation of FAIR principles
Edit/modify steps to close gaps in FAIR principles
Review outputs and document all steps as per high-level requirements.



Outputs

Indicator values
Maps and visualisations
Workflow documentation including validation and uncertainty reports



Impact
Enable reproducibility of existing ecosystem-specific indicators, increase consistency, transparency, and reproducibility across ecosystem assessments. This use case emerged as a high-priority scenario during workshop discussions around workflow adaptability.

Locate suitable workflows in the workflow catalogue.
Verify alignment with assessment or report purpose, adapt if necessary (see UC03, UC04)
Combine outputs and document selection process
Update report metadata including provenance information and references to input workflow (see UC05).



Outputs

Assessment or report with embedded workflows (documented methods and/or outputs)
Workflow citations



Impact
Reduces duplication of effort and accelerates ecosystem assessments. Workshop participants consistently identified workflow adaptability as one of the most important requirements for the EIW project.

Distinguishes applied assessment from workflow development (UC01) and adaptation (UC02, UC03), and places a larger focus on documented limitations and expert review as standard requirements. This use case also brings the consulting and assurance community (UG05) into scope, reflecting the growth of ecosystem accounting and nature-related disclosure obligations.

title: 9  First Tranche (May to Nov 2026)
text:
The first tranche focuses on establishing a minimum viable ecosystem workflow framework that demonstrates adaptability, reproducibility, FAIR compliance and practical applicability across multiple ecosystem indicator use cases. It delivers the foundation required for future workflow expansion while supporting the project’s first reporting milestone and initial workflow deployment activities.
The first objective is to use existing indicator examples as a foundation for developing FAIR reproducible indicator workflows (UC01). Second objective is to use the proposed framework to develop new workflows (UC02).
The modular workflow architecture will have documented swap points for ecosystem type, assessment purpose, indicator variables, and data sources allowing initial exploration of adaptation options (UC03 and UC04).
Special attention will be given to initial implementation of FAIR principles and alignment with PID and FAIR4RS implementation plans whenever practicable, aiming at publication of reproducible workflows (UC05).
Integration of workflows into ongoing or planned assessments will be explored (UC06). It is expected that ongoing asssessments will be the main drivers and motivation for selecting specific ecosystems and purposes for UC02, UC03 and UC04.
This stage will require an initial exploration of options for discoverability (UC07), coupled with requirement gathering steps for Work Package 5.
The development of this tranche will allow initial opportunities for training (UC08) and involvement of early career researchers and students, with a focus on documentation (introductory workflow documentation), development of training material (beginner-friendly quick-start guide), example workflow notebooks and potentially one community event with published workshop outputs.

title: 10  Second Tranche (Jan to Nov 2027)
text:
The second tranche expands the workflow ecosystem beyond individual workflows to support discoverability, scaling, interoperability and broader community adoption. The focus shifts from workflow creation to workflow reuse and operationalisation.
The main objective is to support and expand adaptation of workflows to new ecosystems and different purposes (UC03 and UC04). Development of new indicator workflows (UC02) will be enhanced and driven by ongoing research projects and assessments.
Workflow development in this stage should follow the FAIR4RS and PID implementation plans, including full publication of workflows (UC05).
Integration of workflows into ongoing or planned assessments will continue to be explored (UC06). It is expected that ongoing asssessments will be the main drivers and motivation for selecting specific ecosystems and purposes for UC02, UC03 and UC04.
Scaling up assessment will be coupled with a larger focus on discoverability (UC07) through development of Work Package 5.
The development of this tranche will allow multiple opportunities for training (UC08) and involvement of early career researchers and students. Particularly, the previous experience in development of reproducible indicator workflows from existing workflows (UC01) can be used for didactic purposes. Further development of tiered training materials for beginners, intermediate and advanced users will be complemented with more technical documentation for implementation and maintenance of platform functionality. At least one community event will be completed leading to publication of workshop outputs.

title: 11  Review of Second Tranche Priorities
text:
Consistent with the project plan, second-tranche requirements will be reviewed after the end of Tranche 1 (Nov 2026) and before commencement of Tranche 2 (Jan 2027). The review will evaluate feedback from workflow users, workshop participants, ecosystem experts, and project partners to validate that Year 2 priorities continue to address the most important user needs.
The review will consider:

User adoption and engagement in the initial phases,
Technical performance of workflow reproducibility, data interoperability, expected platform performance, and FAIR compliance.
Community feedback collected through workshops or interviews.
Steering Committee recommendations

Any approved changes to second-tranche priorities will be documented through the project’s governance and change-control processes and reflected in an updated delivery plan.

title: 13  Sustainability
text:
13.1 Custodians and Maintainers
EIW’s workflows, documentation and training materials need to stay usable and accurate after project funding ends. This section sets out who looks after them, how often they are reviewed, and how responsibility is handed over when the project closes.
Each workflow, documentation set and training resource will have:
Custodians are named as organisations rather than individuals, so accountability isn’t lost when staff change. Where possible, each asset has two maintainers, including volunteer maintainers from the user community.
Each asset is labelled Active, Maintenance only (fixes but no new features) or Archived (preserved but no longer updated).

title: 13  Sustainability
14  Workshop Feedbacks:
text:
14.1 Workshop 1
This workshop was designed as a co-design exercise to gather structured feedback from a heterogeneous, multidisciplinary community of end users. Including ecologists, data analysts, coders, and software engineers, on a demo workflow for ecosystem indicator development, as the first in a series of co-design workshops for the Ecosystem Indicators Workflows (EIW) project aimed at ensuring the workflow reflects how people actually work. The workflow follows FAIR principles and supports applications such as ecosystem risk assessment, ecosystem accounting, and the IUCN Green Status, and given the diversity of expertise, institutions, and working practices among users, the workshop set out to understand how people interact with the workflow in practice, tools, preferred data collections, where friction occurs, and what support and collaboration mechanisms are needed to improve usability and adoption.
Familiarity -> ALA CSIRO FED | shape files tabular and RDA | rstudio GIS, GEE, quarto, Jupyter | R python Bash1

title: 14  Workshop Feedbacks:
text:
14.2 Workshop 2
This workshop was a second co-design exercise as a follow-up for the first one, bringing together ecologists, data analysts, coders, and software engineers to improve reproducible workflows for ecosystem indicator development. Where Workshop 1 tested and refined a workflow demo against real-world experience, Workshop 2 shifts focus to scoping and reflection: identifying priority ecosystems, biomes, and functional groups to fill urgent knowledge gaps, surfacing which ecosystems/indicators are most useful for current programs versus future scalability, and assessing how reproducible and reusable participants’ past indicator-development workflows have actually been.
Ecosystems / focus areas nominated for expanding coverage

Oyster Reef of Southern & Eastern Australia12%
Cumberland Plain Woodland, NSW12%
Mangroves of Moreton Bay8%
Saltmarshes of Moreton Bay8%
Alpine snow patch herb fields, SE Australia8%
Coastal lowland rainforests8%
Connected wetlands of the Lake Eyre Basin8%
Georgina gidgee woodlands, Central Australia

Planned future work named by participants (next ~2 years)

Tropical and subtropical rainforests (pending funding)

Yellow Box–White Box–Blakely’s Red Gum and other woodlands (pending funding)

Semi-arid and freshwater ecosystems

Pyric savannas in northern Australia (extending existing Brazil-based indicator work)

Broader RLE/GSE program: compiling existing assessments and building tools to support new ones at scale

This workshop also asked participants to reflect on a past ecosystem-indicator workflow they had personally worked on. The key findings were:

Findability: most participants rated finding the needed data as “moderate” (required searching across sources) to “difficult” (scattered/poorly documented); none rated it “very easy.”

Accessibility: a majority reported data was only “accessible with request/permission” or fully restricted; approx. 71% selected difficulty finding/locating sources as a factor (figure extracted from poll widget — treat as approximate).

Main accessibility blockers reported: complex access procedures, data ownership issues, broken/outdated links, and low-quality metadata. Free-text comments repeatedly cited data-sharing agreements “taking months” and experts “not responding to emails.”

Data readiness challenges: inconsistent classification systems (ecosystem types, species names), varying data quality/resolution, temporal mismatches, and difficulty integrating expert knowledge with quantitative data were the most frequently cited.

Skills required for data preparation: GIS/spatial analysis, remote sensing, and timeseries analysis were most cited, alongside general data cleaning/formatting.

Reproducibility of the calculation step itself: participants were split between “reproducible” and “partially/difficult to reproduce” — several noted that while code for the quantitative portion was reproducible, the expert-elicitation component (setting thresholds) generally was not documented in a reproducible way.

Top priority action nominated to improve reproducibility of the existing workflow: “Strengthen documentation” (most-selected option, ahead of standardising methods, validating with independent data, and increasing technical capacity).

What participants said is needed for the next project to be reproducible from the start: build reproducibility into project design/coding standards from day one rather than as an afterthought; train lead assessors in reproducible coding practices; ensure both accessible data and reproducible compute environments; document species/terminology decisions explicitly.










Topic
Key points
Constraints / challenges
Implications / actions




Workshop 2 outputs
Focus could move beyond single ecosystems to groups of ecosystems to understand how tailored both sets of indicators and individual indicators need to be.
Need to balance general methods across ecosystems with ecosystem-specific adaptation.
Clarify the scale of indicator development: individual ecosystems, ecosystem groups, or cross-ecosystem methods.


Ecosystem focus areas
Tropical and subtropical rainforest, semi-arid woodlands, freshwater ecosystems, and all ecosystems through the Red List of Ecosystems.
Progress depends on existing and pending funding. Most projects are still in early stages, including requirements gathering, indicator exploration, dataset identification, and pilot analyses.
Prioritize projects according to funding status, readiness of datasets, indicators, and whether pilot studies have already been completed.


General constraints
Main constraints are funding and data availability. Datasets need to be collated, cleaned, and harmonized before use in assessments.
Final products must be easy for end users to access, use, and reuse. There is also a tension between user consultation needs and the time required to build infrastructure.
Develop an implementation pathway that combines funding strategy, data preparation, user consultation, and infrastructure design.


Reproducibility of methods and indicators
Core methodologies such as the Red List of Ecosystems are well documented, but reproducible indicators are often lacking.
Indicator execution can remain difficult because coding and programming skills vary among end users.
Provide clear workflows, reusable code, documentation, and user guidance to support reproducible indicator calculation.


Data findability
Data needed for indicators is often difficult to obtain, scattered, and poorly documented. Only a small proportion of participants found the search process moderately difficult.
Search processes vary widely, including search engines, online catalogues, and other sources.
Create clearer guidance on where to find relevant datasets and how to assess their suitability for indicators.


Data accessibility
Nearly half of participants (47%) reported that data was fully open to access, while 27% reported partial access requiring request or permission. The remaining participants reported restricted or inaccessible data.
Access barriers include complex access procedures, data-sharing agreements, difficult database navigation, data ownership issues, broken or outdated links, and low-quality metadata.
Prioritize open and well-documented datasets, while documenting access requirements and known barriers for restricted datasets.


How is the data accessed?
Most data are accessed directly from public repositories (40%) or extracted from published literature, such as supplementary data, printed tables, and figures (25%).
Smaller proportions of participants query specialized databases or use their own data. Downloading spatial data may be complicated.
Explore systems that reduce the need for users to download spatial data manually.


Data readiness & integration
Frequent challenges include varying data resolution and quality, inconsistent classification systems, spatial-scale differences, temporal mismatches, limited metadata, and missing or incomplete data.
These issues make it difficult to align datasets and compare indicators across ecosystems or regions.
Define minimum data standards, harmonization procedures, and metadata requirements for indicator workflows.


Skills required for data preparation
GIS and spatial analysis were reported by 35% of participants as required skills, while data cleaning and formatting were reported by 29%.
Ecological survey knowledge is important to ensure that data are used correctly, including understanding whether similar variables are measuring the same thing. Knowledge of species names, synonyms, and name changes is also important.
Support users with training, templates, and guidance covering spatial analysis, data cleaning, ecological assumptions, and taxonomy.


Reproducibility
Indicator calculation was considered partially reproducible by 67% of participants, while the remaining participants considered it difficult to reproduce.
Limits include a lack of documented processes and validation points, data availability, limited time to engage with managers, difficulty integrating expert knowledge, and variable data quality.
Strengthen documentation, validation checkpoints, data provenance, and mechanisms for incorporating expert knowledge.


Next steps
All participants highlighted stronger documentation as the priority of action for improving workflow reproducibility.
Important methodological details can be lost when workflows are only reported in scientific papers.
Develop complete documentation that captures assumptions, data sources, processing steps, code, validation checks, and decision points.
